title: Searching
learningGoals: write a binary search on a sorted array
explain why binary search needs sorted data

youtube.title: C++ Searching: Linear and Binary Search | C++ Programming EP 39
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a linear search, write a binary search on a sorted array and explain why binary search needs sorted data, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Searching · 0:51 Linear search · 1:31 Binary search steps · 2:02 Second program · 3:02 Recap · 3:32 Bug of the Day · 4:20 Challenge · 4:40 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "FIND IT FAST" in tomato on butter; Xecxec next to a crab with a magnifying glass at a library shelf; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a crab with a magnifying glass at a library shelf

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we search. One method is simple. The other is clever, and it finds one item among a million in about twenty steps.

scenes.onScreen: "Searching": numbered lines (1. Linear search checks each item; 2. Binary search halves the range each time; 3. Binary search needs sorted data) and an analogy card: a dictionary: you open it in the middle, then choose the left or the right half
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Linear search checks the items one by one, from the start. It works on any data, but it can be slow. Binary search needs sorted data. It looks at the middle item, and then it throws away half of the range. Think of a dictionary. You open it in the middle, then you pick the left or the right half.
points: Binary search halves the range each time

analogy.title: Searching
analogy.body: A dictionary: you open it in the middle, then choose the left or the right half

scenes.onScreen: linear.cpp: a function that returns the index of a value
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The loop checks each index from zero. [HL 6] If the item equals the target, [HL 7] the function returns that index at once. [HL 10] If the loop ends, the value is not there. We return minus one. [HL 15] Three is at index three. [HL 16] Four is not in the array, so the answer is minus one.

scenes.onScreen: a table: low, high, middle and the decision for each step
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here is a binary search for five in the sorted list one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen. Step one looks at the middle item, seven. Five is smaller, so go left. Step two looks at three. Five is bigger, so go right. Step three finds five. Only three steps were needed.

diagram.caption: a table: low, high, middle and the decision for each step

scenes.onScreen: binary.cpp: binary search on a sorted array
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Low and high mark the part of the array that is still possible. [HL 7] Mid is the middle index. [HL 8] If the middle item is the target, we are done. [HL 11] If it is too small, we move low past mid. [HL 13] If it is too big, we move high below mid. [HL 16] When low passes high, the target is not there.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as binary dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints two.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Linear search checks the items one by one. Two. Binary search halves the range each time. Three. Binary search needs sorted data. Four. Both return minus one when the value is missing. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Linear search checks the items one by one.
Binary search halves the range each time.
Both return minus one when the value is missing.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Binary search on unsorted data
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The array holds three, but the search says minus one. The array is not sorted. Binary search looks at nine in the middle. Nine is bigger than three, so it throws away the right half. But the three was in the right half. Sort the array first.

scenes.onScreen: I use binary search to find my socks. Half of the drawer is always wrong.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I use binary search to find my socks. Half of the drawer is always wrong.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: search for a name
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a linear search that finds a name in an array of five strings. Print the index, or minus one. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 40 · Sorting: bubble and selection
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: sorting, bubble and selection. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

-1
bug.why: Binary search throws away half of the range using the order of the items. If the items are not in order, it throws away the wrong half.

pun: "I use binary search to find my socks. Half of the drawer is always wrong."
challenge: Write a linear search that finds a name in an array of five strings. Print the index, or minus one.
challengeAnswer: Loop over the array. If the item equals the target string, return its index. After the loop, return minus one.
